en: Each painter has a style made of four numbers: hue, brush size, complexity and angularity. These numbers generate a small abstract painting for the gallery. Similar styles produce similar-looking paintings.

Each round, every painter at the same time copies half of another painter's style with the copy rate probability. Otherwise they innovate, randomly changing their own style by the amount of originality.

Whom to copy is influenced by popularity. Popularity rises with the number of people who copied a painter (and fades over time), and the larger the popularity bias, the more often popular painters are chosen.
Diversity is the average style distance between pairs of painters (maximum 1), and concentration is the share of painters close to the most popular style.
Copy rate <output id="o-copy"></output>
At 100%, everyone copies someone every round
Popularity bias <output id="o-bias"></output>
The larger it is, the more often popular painters get copied
Originality <output id="o-originality"></output>
How much a style changes when painters innovate
Same settings, new gallery
① The Gallery
Each picture is one painter. The gold outline marks the most popular painter, and a green outline marks painters who tried a new style this round. Watch whether the pictures grow more alike.
② Diversity and Concentration Over Time
The blue line is diversity (how different the styles are) and the gold line is concentration (the share following the popular style).
Diversity
Style concentration
③ Style Map
The horizontal axis is hue and the vertical axis is complexity; each dot is one painter. When the dots pile into one place, the painters have converged on one style. Larger dots are more popular.
④ As the Copy Rate Rises
The horizontal axis is the copy rate and the vertical axis is diversity (blue) and concentration (gold) after 80 rounds. The gray line is diversity with no popularity bias. Dots are 4 runs.

What it shows: The higher the copy rate, the less diverse the styles become and the more they pile onto a single "house style." In this model there is no single sudden collapse point; diversity falls continuously, and concentration rises sharply between copy rates of about 40% and 80%. A bias toward copying popular painters makes concentration much larger at the same copy rate, and with low originality even a moderate copy rate hardens into one style.

What it doesn't show: This does not reproduce real image-generating AI or how painters actually behave. It is a very simple model of cultural transmission that reduces style to four numbers and keeps only "copying" and "random innovation," and the pictures are decorative abstracts drawn from those numbers. It also does not claim that copying is bad or that originality is always good: copying spreads skills and can nurture good styles.

A cultural-transmission model of how copying and originality affect diversity, inspired by the experiment of Salganik, Dodds, Watts (2006), Science 311, on how social influence changes the predictability of success, and by cultural-evolution research. It is this project's own design and does not reproduce a paper's numbers.

The popularity bias sets the weight of being chosen to (1 - bias) + bias × (popularity / mean popularity)². An earlier version used popularity directly, but then the bias slider barely affected results, so it was squared. We also tested a chance for innovators to be "noticed" and gain popularity (a novelty reward), but concentration stayed at about 52–58%, so it was left out of the interface.

Diversity is the pairwise average of the distance across the four numbers (hue is circular, so its largest distance is 0.5), scaled to 0–1. The random start is about 0.44, and results use the average of the last 20 rounds. You can verify with node tools/validate-painters.js.
The code is available on GitHub.
Why Do Incompetent Bosses Exist? · Simulatio Lab
Does promoting your best performer make an organization better? Compare promotion methods under the Peter principle.
Promoting your best performer seems obvious. But what if "being good at one job says nothing about the next"? Compare promotion methods and organizational efficiency in a 160-person company.
A 6-level pyramid with 1, 5, 11, 21, 41 and 81 people from top to bottom. Each person has a competence (0–10) shown by color (red is low, blue is high).
Each year, people who reach 60 retire and the vacancy is filled by someone promoted from the level below. The bottom level is filled by new hires.
In the common-sense hypothesis (continuity 100%), competence stays the same after promotion. In the Peter hypothesis (continuity 0%), competence in the new job is drawn fresh.
Choose the promotion method: best performer / worst performer / random / alternating. Efficiency is the average competence per level, weighted more for higher levels.

④ Comparing Promotion Methods
Average efficiency from 12 runs of each method over the current duration. Blue is the common-sense hypothesis, red is the Peter hypothesis.
Common sense (continuity 100%)
Peter hypothesis (continuity 0%)

What it shows: "Promote whoever is good at the job" works only if competence carries over after promotion. If competence in the new role is independent, promoting only the top performers gives below-average results. The promotion criterion should be "can they do the new job well?" rather than "are they good at the current job?"
